newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Gloom hangs over Vietnam's energy industry.
newsitem.headline: Gloom hangs over Vietnam's energy industry.

text.p: A spat with China over potentially gas-rich waters, acrimony over scuppered plans for a refinery with foreign partners and disappointing offshore oil finds cast a gloom over Vietnam's annual oil and gas show on Monday.

As industry executives gathered in this southern city for a two-day conference and three-day trade exhibition, attention was firmly focused on an unexplored area off central Vietnam in the South China Sea where China started drilling earlier this month.

Although Hanoi protested when China first drilled there in 1993, analysts said the uncharacteristic public protest this time may reflect growing anxiety about energy resources following a string of disappointments.
Vu Van Mao, a director at the state oil and gas firm Petrovietnam, told reporters the area was unquestionably within Vietnamese territory and said the Chinese rig must be withdrawn.

"Our government considers that China is violating the Vietnamese continental shelf and our government is asking China to pull out," he said, ruling out joint exploitation of the area by the two countries.

"They (Vietnam) are very keen to make sure they get everything they can these days," said the country manager of one western oil and gas firm, who declined to be named. "There has been much less oil than people expected in the early days."
With its crude oil production rising to more than eight million tonnes in 1987 from next to nothing a decade earlier, Vietnam has long been seen as a new energy frontier.
But an initial burst of foreign investment worth some $2 billion has been followed by a stream of bad news.

Australia's Broken Hill Pty has been caught up in a dispute with the government over the terms of its contract at the Dai Hung field since estimates of reserves were slashed to as little as 100 million barrels from up to 800 million.

Royal Dutch Shell last year allowed a production-sharing contract (PSC) off the southern coast to expire. Officials at the Anglo-Dutch oil major said that after sinking $150-160 million into offshore exploration here, Shell was taking a "more realistic view of Vietnam".
"We are not jumping up and saying that this is an El Dorado," said Shell Vietnam general manager Nguyen Quoc Khanh.
Keen to limit growing oil-product imports, Vietnam has sought to build its own refinery, but those plans have also run into problems.

France's Total pulled out of the $1.3 billion project in 1995, calling it "economically unviable", because the refinery was to be built in an undeveloped area far from the country's oil fields and main consumer markets.
A consortium of mostly Asian companies took Total's place, but it fell apart earlier this year in a dispute with Petrovietnam over terms.
Petrovietnam has since vowed to go it alone on the refinery, though analysts say it is not clear where the money would come from or whether it will be built by the year 2000 as planned.
One positive note for Vietnam is natural gas, which is shifting the focus away from crude oil.
Hanoi has estimated Vietnam's gas reserves at a huge 1.3 trillion cubic metres and potential annual output by 2010 at 14 billion cubic metres.
That could meet demand in Vietnam's growing domestic market, which the plan puts at about 8.0 billion cubic metres in 15 years, and still leave some for export.
